intro: A small rocking figure grows into repeated chords spanning the keyboard, then returns after a passage of faster decoration. Listen for the difference between the melody’s pace and the activity surrounding it.
question: How does a quiet rhythmic figure acquire the weight of a climax?

sections.label: Opening · Lento
sections.mNote: rocking figure and sustained chordal answers

sections.label: Central expansion · pesante
sections.mNote: repeated chords enlarge the rhythmic cell

cues.title: A rocking cell
cues.text: The opening places short groups of three notes beside sustained chords. Follow the recurring rhythm rather than expecting a continuous tune: repetition binds together phrases separated by rests and resonance.
cues.evidence: The Gutheil score, reprinted by Boosey & Hawkes, p. 92, shows the triplet figure and tied chordal answers. The analysis places the opening in a quiet range, about −34 to −28 dB through 0:25; no individual attack is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Completing twenty-four keys
cues.text: The thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in 1910, complete Rachmaninoff’s coverage of all twenty-four major and minor keys. The earlier ten of Op. 23 and the single C♯ minor Prelude supply the other eleven.
cues.evidence: IMSLP’s work catalogue identifies the 1910 set, its keys and its relationship to Opp. 23 and 3: https://imslp.org/wiki/13_Preludes,_Op.32_(Rachmaninoff,_Sergei)

cues.title: Follow the middle voice
cues.text: Through the opening’s expansion, listen inside the chords as well as above them. Rachmaninoff passes the moving figure between registers; a sustained upper note can leave an inner line to carry the phrase forward.
cues.evidence: Score p. 92 distributes the figure between the hands and registers. Relative level rises around 1:05–1:20, but the report does not isolate individual voices.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Weight without a new instrument
cues.text: The central expansion replaces the opening’s separated gestures with repeated chords. The marking “pesante” asks for weight: a single piano supplies both the continuing pulse and the long line emerging from it.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 92–93 supplies pesante and the chordal expansion. The provisional join at 1:44 sits among boundaries at 1:40, 1:44 and 1:52; level rises from −25.5 dB at 1:40 to −8.6 at 1:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A remembered conversation
cues.text: Pianist Benno Moiseiwitsch recalled Rachmaninoff associating this Prelude with Arnold Böcklin’s painting The Return. The link comes through Moiseiwitsch’s testimony; the published score has no pictorial subtitle.
cues.evidence: The account is cited to Bertensson and Leyda, Sergei Rachmaninoff: A Lifetime in Music, p. 296, in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preludes,_Op._32_(Rachmaninoff). The inspected score bears only the generic Prelude heading.

cues.title: The crest gives way
cues.text: Around the middle of the recording, the sustained chordal pressure gives way to a much quieter stretch. Keep the earlier rhythmic cell in mind while the texture makes more room around each line.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows cluster at 2:15–2:35. Level falls from −7.5 dB at 2:35 to −33.6 at 2:45; the strongest boundary is 2:48. This supports a broad withdrawal, not an exact bar onset.

cues.title: Decoration and sustained notes
cues.text: In the passage after the central crest, distinguish the held notes from the smaller figures moving around them. The score increases the decorative activity without making every note a new melodic destination.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 94–95 develops groups of six, seven and then rapid scalar notes around sustained tones. The report shows renewed activity and a smaller swell around 3:10–3:35, supporting passage-level placement only.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A credited modern performance
cues.text: This recording is by the pianist who publishes as La Pianista, made on 12 May 2010. The performer released the recording under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; the separate public-domain notice concerns the composition.
cues.evidence: The Commons file description explicitly separates “For the Recording” from “For the Composition” and names the performer and performance date: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rachmaninoff_Prelude_in_B_Minor,_Op._32,_No._10.oga

cues.title: Recognition after the detour
cues.text: In the later recollection, compare the rocking figure with its first appearance. The same shape follows a large chordal climax and a decorated passage; its return does not require another increase in volume.
cues.evidence: Score p. 95 marks the opening material “a tempo, come prima”. The quieter stretch after 3:45 and local B-minor estimates support the approximate return at 3:50; the report cannot establish its first bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Low notes and space
cues.text: The close leaves increasing space around the bass and final chords. Follow the distance between a fresh attack and the resonance that remains, rather than treating the quiet ending as an unfinished climax.
cues.evidence: The last system of score p. 95 supplies low B, widely spaced harmonies and a final held sonority. A boundary at 4:42 precedes the low-activity closing region; level falls below −39 dB around 4:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Let the resonance finish
cues.text: The last sound continues after the pianist’s final attack. Listen to that remaining resonance as a separate part of the ending: the phrase can have arrived while the piano is still audible.
cues.evidence: No onsets are detected from 5:10 to the file’s 5:21 end; level decreases from −42.8 to −51.5 dB. This describes the final decay, not the precise release of a key or pedal.

transitions.title: The small figure becomes repeated chords
transitions.how: The opening’s triplet cell survives the change of scale. At the pesante passage, chordal repetitions take over the pulse while a long bass F♯ supports the growing weight. Rachmaninoff asks for a gradual crescendo and then restores Tempo I for the fuller chordal writing. The join is an enlargement of rhythm and register, not the arrival of a separate melody unrelated to the opening.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 92–93: pesante, repeated triplet chords, low F♯ and crescendo. Analysis boundaries at 1:40–1:52 and the associated level rise place the join provisionally at 1:44.

transitions.title: Chordal weight loosens into separate lines
transitions.how: A written diminuendo, slowing and fermata interrupt the force of the repeated chords. The next passage, marked L’istesso tempo, begins quietly with sustained upper notes and a less solidly chordal accompaniment. The pace need not collapse: Rachmaninoff changes the density and distribution of attacks, then lets increasingly small note-values animate the space between the sustained notes.
transitions.evidence: The end of score p. 93 and beginning of p. 94 show the diminuendo, fermata and L’istesso tempo. Analysis drops by more than 25 dB across 2:35–2:45 and gives its strongest boundary at 2:48.

transitions.title: The running line releases the opening
transitions.how: Rapid figures traverse the keyboard and diminish towards a held point. After the fermata, “a tempo, come prima” brings back the opening’s rocking cell and tied chordal answers. The decorative rush does not become a new theme: its function is to clear space for recognition, restoring the original phrase shape and B-minor setting.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 95 places the fast passage, diminuendo and fermata before the explicit return. The analysis’s low point at 3:45 and quieter 3:50–4:10 region support this estimated 3:50 join, not a bar-aligned return.

transitions.title: The bass anchors the closing chords
transitions.how: The recollected phrase shortens into closing gestures. Rachmaninoff separates low bass notes from higher chords and slows the succession of attacks; the final B-based sonority is allowed to resonate under a fermata. Register and spacing now provide the breadth previously produced by repeated chords.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 95, last two systems, supplies the separated bass and final held sonority. The 4:42 analysis boundary and sparse 4:45–5:10 attacks locate a closing region rather than a precise final cadence.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
